clue.text: One should not have it after a close shave.

definitions.text: One should not have it after a close shave

parts.note: the surface reading: something you hope to be spared, like a scratch after a narrow escape
the setter's reading: a literal shave with a razor, after which the face should be smooth

explanation.walkthrough: A 'close shave' is idiom for a narrow escape, but here it is taken literally: after shaving closely there should be no bristly regrowth left on the chin.
explanation.definitionFit: Stubble is the short bristly hair on an unshaven face, exactly what a good razor removes.

clue.text: This suggests the time before the taxi and is proverbially sluggish.

parts.words: This suggests the time before the taxi
parts.note: read as two words, 'cab age': the era of horse-drawn cabs before the motor taxi
a dull, inert person is called a vegetable, this one above all

explanation.surface: A puzzle about old horse-cab days and something famously slow.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a sound-and-split joke, CAB AGE, the days of horse cabs; the spelling has an extra B, so it only 'suggests' the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabbage is the stock image of a dull, inactive person, so calling someone one means they are torpid.

clue.text: "Who would fardels bear, to — and sweat under a weary life?"
It looks as if this enthusiast should keep a cool head.

definitions.text: It looks as if this enthusiast should keep a cool head

parts.note: the surface reading: a zealot who is told to stay calm
the setter's reading: the written word looks like a fan plus attic, and the attic is slang for the head, which a fan would keep cool

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as FAN + ATIC: an electric fan in the 'attic', old slang for the head, would keep that head cool.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanatic is a person filled with excessive, single-minded zeal for a cause, an extreme enthusiast.

clue.text: Here the page introduces the show.

parts.note: the surface reading: a pageboy or a programme page announcing a performance
the setter's reading: the word page literally stands at the start of the answer

explanation.surface: A page boy announcing the start of a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer opens with the letters of 'page'; the remaining ANT is not clued, so this is a hint rather than full wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pageant is an elaborate public show or procession, often of historical scenes.

clue.text: This starts a shindy — even when it isn't barked.

definitions.note: the definition is the 'it': a body part that gets barked, that is scraped

indicators.note: the opening letters of the following word are the ones wanted, lifted from its front

parts.note: the first four letters of shindy, a noisy row

explanation.surface: A scraped leg sparking a row, or a row starting even without one.
explanation.walkthrough: A shindy is a noisy quarrel; to bark a leg is to scrape the skin off it on something hard.
explanation.definitionFit: The front of the lower leg is the part most often barked against furniture or a step.

clue.text: One letter more than in volume five.

definitions.text: One letter more than in volume five
definitions.note: no separate definition: the whole clue is wordplay, settled by the crossings

parts.note: taken as written
VOL is the standard abbreviation for volume
V is the Roman numeral for five
a single extra letter, unspecified, is added at the end to make a word

explanation.surface: A librarian counting letters in the fifth volume of a set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In vol. V' gives INVOLV, and one letter more completes a word; the clue gives no separate definition, and the crossings settle it.
explanation.definitionFit: To involve is to include or entangle something as a part, as a book's fifth volume includes its contents.

clue.text: This general pardon seems to include the pigs.

parts.note: the surface reading: a pardon so general that even the farm animals are let off
the setter's reading: the written word ends in a sty, the pigs' pen

explanation.surface: A pardon so sweeping it even covers the pigs.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer ends in STY, the pen where pigs live, so the word 'includes the pigs'; the other letters are not clued.
explanation.definitionFit: An amnesty is an official pardon granted to a whole class of offenders at once.

parts.note: the surface reading: a lake or park celebrated for a bird
the setter's reading: the capital S marks a nickname, Ben Jonson's tribute to Shakespeare as the sweet swan of his home river

explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson called Shakespeare the 'Sweet Swan of Avon', after the river through Stratford; the capital S is the clue's only hint that the swan is a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: The river at Stratford is celebrated because Shakespeare, its 'swan', was born on its banks.

clue.text: You will not solve this without one.

definitions.text: You will not solve this without one

parts.note: the surface reading: a warning about this very clue
the setter's reading: any problem needs a notion of how to crack it

explanation.walkthrough: The clue talks about itself: no puzzle gets solved without a notion of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea is a thought or notion in the mind, the thing a solver needs before any problem gives way.

clue.text: Patriarch much honoured in the nursery.

definitions.note: no separate definition: the anagram material stands for the whole clue

indicators.note: the bracketed abbreviation states outright that the words before it are to be rearranged

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter as the material to rearrange

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale image of dragons lying in their lairs.
explanation.walkthrough: Early puzzles sometimes clued an answer by anagram alone with no definition; the crossing letters confirm it.
explanation.definitionFit: Girandoles are branched candlesticks, or revolving firework wheels, a word taken from Italian.

clue.text: It's unwise to marry in this.

definitions.text: It's unwise to marry in this

parts.note: the surface reading: perhaps a place or a month thought unlucky for weddings
the setter's reading: the proverb 'marry in a hurry, repent at leisure', here using its usual noun

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'Marry in haste, repent at leisure'; the clue reads like a superstition about a month or place.
explanation.definitionFit: Haste is excessive speed or hurry, the state the proverb warns against wedding in.

clue.text: There is not one at the Naval Conference.

definitions.text: There is not one at the Naval Conference

parts.note: the surface reading: some delegate absent from the talks
the setter's reading: a landlocked nation with no navy had no reason to attend the 1930 London Naval Conference

explanation.walkthrough: The London Naval Conference of 1930 was in the news when this puzzle ran; Switzerland, being landlocked, has no navy to send.
explanation.definitionFit: A Swiss is a person from Switzerland, a country with no coastline and no navy.

clue.text: There are men in this strait.

parts.note: the surface reading: sailors on ships in a stretch of sea
the setter's reading: these letters literally sit at the start of the name

explanation.surface: A narrow sea passage with men aboard ships in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Menai Strait separates Anglesey from mainland Wales, and its name begins with MEN; the remaining AI is not clued.
explanation.definitionFit: The Menai Strait is the narrow channel between the island of Anglesey and north-west Wales.

clue.text: This urchin always has a friend with him of his own nationality.

parts.words: always has a friend with him
parts.note: the surface reading: a street child who is never without a pal
the setter's reading: the French word for friend, ami, sits inside the French word for a street urchin

explanation.surface: A street boy who always goes around with a pal from home.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is French, and inside it sits AMI, French for friend, so the friend is 'of his own nationality'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamin is a street urchin, a ragged child of the streets, a word borrowed from French.

clue.text: You should get this if you have the will.

definitions.text: You should get this if you have the will

parts.note: the surface reading: a legacy owed to someone named in a will
the setter's reading: the proverb 'where there's a will there's a way', will meaning determination

explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' suggests a legal testament and an inheritance; it is determination, from the proverb 'where there's a will there's a way'.
explanation.definitionFit: A route is a way or course to a destination, the 'way' the proverb promises.

clue.text: This one is not permanent, for it means to give up.

parts.note: a hair wave that is set by hand rather than a permanent wave (a perm) does not last

explanation.surface: A hairdresser warning that a styling will not last and must be surrendered.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue pictures a hair wave that is not a 'permanent', and the answer is spelt differently from that wave though it is said the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To waive a right or claim is to give it up voluntarily, to relinquish it.

clue.text: Byron wrote a poem about him.

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone willing to take a new surname for love.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: falling in love leads to marriage, and once a bride took her husband's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamour is to fill with love, the feeling that once led a bride to change her surname at marriage.

clue.text: Here you want a beginner, there's one in the middle of the pier.

indicators.note: something set in the middle of another thing is enclosed by it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone on a seaside pier looking for a novice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here you want' and 'there's' are old-style padding; 'in the middle of' means the word one splits pier exactly in half.
explanation.definitionFit: A pioneer is one who opens up new ground, the first in a field, so a beginner in that sense.
